name: Changuena
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Chibchan language of Panama; only 19th-c. wordlists (Pinart 1890, Brinton 1891) and Constenla classification notes

sources.citation: Pinart, Alphonse L. 1900. Notes sur les tribus indiennes de famille guarano-guaymies de l'isthme de Panama et du Centre-Amérique. Paris: Imprimerie Durand.
sources.note: Ethnohistorical notes with a comparative vocabulary table that has DORASQUE and CHANGUINA columns; no remark on accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/tonique empty; scanned of the table is garbled).

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1891. The American Race. New York: N. D. C. Hodges, pp. 174-175.
sources.note: Ethnographic paragraph and tribe list for the 'Changuina linguistic stock'; nothing linguistic beyond a few Pinart words.

sources.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 1985. Las lenguas dorasque y chánguena y sus relaciones genealógicas. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 11(2): 81-91.
sources.note: Comparative/classification study. p. 82: the only surviving Chánguena data are Pinart's 134 forms. No mention of accent/stress anywhere; p. 90 says the materials still need to be interpreted phonologically (no phonological analysis exists).
sources.venue: Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1891. Vocabularies from the Musquito Coast. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 29(135): 1-4.
sources.note: Compares Rama with 12 Changuina words taken from Pinart 1890; nothing on stress.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society

sources.citation: Pinart, Alphonse L. 1890. Vocabulario castellano-dorasque: dialectos chumulu, gualaca y changuina. Petite Bibliothèque Américaine II. Paris: Ernest Leroux. 42 pp.
sources.note: Wordlist only (Changuina forms marked C.); 3-page NOTA is historical. Acute accents are written on many forms (C. ndálahoi 'adios', kaí 'aguacate', kókri 'gallina', sópi 'gallinazo', siúe 'gente blanca', rubúi 'gente negra', cúlit) on varying syllables, but there is no statement about accent or stress.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page chan1324 (Changuena) and Glottolog hh.bib entries 103859, 125334, 126354, 150067
sources.note: Lists only Pinart 1890, Brinton 1891 (x2), Constenla 1985 and Constenla 2012 (Chibchan languages, survey chapter); no grammar or phonology reference exists.
Nothing on phonology; cites only Constenla 1985 and Glottolog.

sources.citation: Pache, Matthias J. 2018. Contributions to Chibchan historical linguistics. Doctoral thesis, Universiteit Leiden (Leiden University Centre for Linguistics), 5 December 2018. Section 2.3.7 'Chánguena', pp. 317-319 (2.3.7.1.1 'Chánguena vowels and suprasegmentals', p. 318; Table 31 Chánguena vowels, Table 32 Chánguena consonants).

tone.quote: The only source on Chánguena is Pinart (1890), which amounts to a wordlist of Chánguena and the two Dorasque dialects Chumulu and Gualaca. It reveals much less data on Chánguena than on Dorasque. ... Pinart (1890) also gives additional symbols such as the acute accent in several words. It may refer to stress and/or tone in Chánguena. The macron, attested in some cases on <ō> or <ū>, may have indicated vowel length in Chánguena. It is unclear whether or not italics in some Chánguena vowels may have referred to nasality, for instance in <ma> ‘chicha’ or to non-syllabic realization in <keu> ‘fire’.
tone.locator: pp. 317-318, section 2.3.7 'Chánguena' and 2.3.7.1.1 'Chánguena vowels and suprasegmentals' (below Table 31)
tone.summary: None describable: the source states only that Pinart's acute accents may mark stress and/or tone and macrons may mark length; five vowel graphemes i e a o u; no tone inventory, TBU, or stress rule can be recovered from the 19th-century wordlist.
